opus-5.5.text:
I think they're actually really tightly linked. People sometimes frame safety and usefulness as a trade-off, but for agents, I'd argue you can't get real usefulness without safety. If you want an agent that can go off and do research for you for twenty or thirty minutes, or eventually take actions like sending emails, making purchases, or editing documents, you have to be able to trust it. If you don't, you end up babysitting it and checking every step, and then it's not saving you any time.

With something like a research agent, the risks are relatively contained. It's mostly reading and synthesizing information, so the main concerns are accuracy, citing sources properly, and not being misled by bad information on the web. Once agents start taking actions in the world, the stakes go up a lot. Some actions are hard to reverse. You can't unsend an email or un-buy something easily. And there are new attack surfaces, like prompt injection, where a webpage or document the agent reads tries to hijack it into doing something you never asked for.

So a lot of what we think about is how to give the model good judgment about when to proceed on its own and when to check in with the user. You want it to be autonomous enough to be useful, but to confirm before anything consequential or irreversible. Getting that balance right matters. If it asks permission for everything it's annoying, and if it never asks it's dangerous.

I think over time, as models get more reliable and we build better safeguards, monitoring, and ways for users to set preferences, people will become comfortable delegating more and more. But that trust has to be earned, and safety is really the foundation that makes the whole vision of agents work.

r001.rationale: The candidate says agents must be trusted to handle delegated research and actions, and that without trust users must babysit them. It also notes safeguards against actions the user never requested, conveying that usefulness depends on avoiding unwanted side effects.

fable-5.1.text:
I actually think safety and usefulness are much more intertwined than people tend to assume. If you're going to hand an agent your browser, your email, your credentials, and ask it to go book a trip or do a week of research for you, you have to trust it. And trust isn't just "did it get the answer right," it's "did it take the actions I would have wanted, did it stop and ask when something was ambiguous, did it avoid doing something irreversible when it wasn't sure."

So from where I sit, a lot of the work that looks like safety work is really what makes these things usable at all. A model that will happily follow instructions it finds on a random webpage, or that will delete a file because it misread the task, is not a useful agent. Nobody is going to delegate anything meaningful to it. Things like prompt injection robustness, knowing when to pause before a purchase or a send, being honest about what it actually did versus what it tried to do, those are the features that let you expand the scope of what you delegate.

The other thing I'd say is that the failure mode for agents is different from chat. In chat, if the model says something wrong, you read it and you correct it. With an agent that's running for twenty minutes and taking actions, you might not be watching, so the model's own judgment is doing a lot more of the work. That's why we spend so much time on things like having the model surface uncertainty at the right moment rather than plowing ahead, and on confirming before anything that's hard to undo. Those feel like constraints, but they're actually what lets you turn the autonomy up.

Where I think it gets genuinely hard is the tradeoff curve. If an agent asks you about everything, it's annoying and you stop using it. If it asks about nothing, it eventually does something you really didn't want. Getting that calibration right, where it has good taste about what matters, is in some sense the whole product. So I don't see safety as a tax on capability. For agents in particular, I think it's closer to the thing that unlocks the capability being worth anything.

r001.rationale: The response says meaningful delegation requires trusting the agent to take the actions the user wants, pause when uncertain, and avoid unwanted or irreversible actions; it links that trust directly to usefulness.

astra-6.text:
I think safety and usefulness are really closely connected for agents. If you’re going to delegate something to an agent, you need to trust that it understands what you want, stays within the scope you’ve given it, and checks with you when there’s a consequential decision that you should make.

For a research task, that might mean being clear about uncertainty and giving you enough evidence to assess its conclusions. Once it can take actions, you also care about what it’s allowed to do and whether you can undo a mistake. There’s a big difference between drafting an email and sending it.

The challenge is getting those boundaries right without making the agent ask permission for every little step. You want it to work independently where you’re comfortable delegating, and bring you in where your judgment matters. Getting that right is a big part of making agents useful.

r001.rationale: The response says delegation requires trusting the agent to understand the request and stay within its scope, and discusses limiting actions and undoing mistakes. This communicates trust in carrying out delegated tasks without unwanted side effects.

sol-6.1.text:
I think safety and usefulness are really closely connected here. If an agent is going to research something and then take actions on your behalf, you need to trust that it understands what you want, that it’s operating within the permissions you’ve given it, and that it knows when to come back and ask you a question.

There’s a big difference between an agent finding a flight and actually booking it. You want it to do as much of the work as possible, but you also want control over the consequential decisions. And on the research side, you want to understand what evidence it’s using and where it’s uncertain.

So I think a lot of making these systems safer is also what makes them useful enough to delegate to. If you have to watch every step because you’re worried it might do something unexpected, you haven’t really saved much time.

r001.rationale: The response says delegation is useful only if the agent can be trusted to follow permissions and avoid unexpected actions; otherwise, the user must watch every step and saves little time.
